instructions:
A PDF was filed by hand. Open the file at `attachments.pdf_path` and read it, then produce a structured summary.

Read it as a document, not as text: look at the figures, tables and plots. A result table usually settles what the paper actually achieved faster than the prose does, and a figure often carries the method. If the document is long, read the abstract, introduction, method and results sections in full and skim the rest.

`bibliography` must come from the document itself — its title page, header or footer. The filename is not evidence; it is whatever the person who saved the file happened to type.

`topics` is your judgement. These are the topics this archive tracks; list the slugs this paper genuinely belongs to, and leave the list empty rather than forcing a fit:
- reasoning-evaluation: Reasoning Evaluation — Benchmarks for reasoning and the methodology behind them: what each one actually tests, how contamination and memorization inflate a score, and where a reported gain fails to reproduce. The question the archive answers is which numbers a claim about reasoning can be built on.
- reasoning-faithfulness: Reasoning Faithfulness — The gap between a model's stated chain of thought and the computation that produced its answer: unfaithful or post-hoc rationalization, reasoning that is latent rather than written, encoded or steganographic traces, and what a monitor reading the trace can and cannot catch. The question the archive answers is when a visible reasoning trace is evidence about the model, and when it is only text.
- reasoning-interpretability: Reasoning Interpretability — What the computation behind reasoning looks like from the inside: circuits and the attention heads that carry them, features recovered by sparse dictionary learning, and the causal interventions used to establish that a component or a written state matters. The question the archive answers is which claims about a model's internal reasoning the available intervention methods can actually support, and at what granularity.
- reasoning-training: Reasoning Training — How a language model acquires long-form reasoning: reinforcement learning against verifiable rewards, process versus outcome supervision, distillation of reasoning traces, and self-training. The question the archive answers is which training signal produces reasoning that generalizes, and what each one costs.
- test-time-scaling: Test-Time Scaling — What a model gains by thinking longer at inference: sampling and verification, search over reasoning steps, self-correction, and the length of the chain itself as a compute knob. The question the archive answers is how accuracy trades against tokens spent, and where that curve flattens.

`relevance` must have one entry per slug you listed in `topics`.

Then set `read_from`: 'document' if you opened the file, 'abstract' if you did not and worked from the payload. Say which you actually did. A reading that is honest about being abstract-only can be redone later; one that claims a document it never opened cannot be found at all.

Rules:
- Write in en.
- Ground every statement in the supplied material. If something is not stated,
  leave the field empty rather than inferring it.
- No marketing language. Prefer the specific number over the adjective.
- Return one JSON object matching the schema exactly. No prose around it.

bibliography.abstract: string - the paper's own abstract, verbatim
bibliography.arxiv_id: string - arXiv id if printed on the document, else empty
authors: string - author name, in the order printed
bibliography.doi: string - DOI if printed on the document, else empty
bibliography.title: string - the paper's own title, exactly as printed
bibliography.venue: string - journal, conference or 'preprint'; empty if unclear
bibliography.year: integer - publication year, 0 if the document does not say

concepts: string - reusable ideas this paper relies on or introduces
datasets: string - datasets, benchmarks, corpora or simulators used. Not models: a checkpoint that was evaluated or fine-tuned belongs in `models`.
output_schema.limitations: string - stated limits plus any the reader should notice
output_schema.method: string - how it works, enough for a reader to explain it
methods: string - named methods, architectures or algorithms
models: string - models the work trains, evaluates or analyses, as named in the paper (e.g. a base checkpoint, a released reasoning model, a judge)
output_schema.one_liner: string - what the paper does, in one sentence, no hype
output_schema.problem: string - the problem it addresses and why it is open
output_schema.read_from: string - required: 'document' if you opened the attached PDF and read it, 'abstract' if you worked from the payload alone. Answer for what you did, not for what you were asked to do

relevance.<topic-slug>: string - why this matters for that specific topic

output_schema.results: string - headline numbers, on which benchmarks, against what
topics: string - slug of a tracked topic this paper belongs to; omit any that do not genuinely apply

payload.title: Signal for Reasoning Dynamics in Large Language Models

bibliography.abstract: Recent work has sought to understand Large Language Models (LLMs) reasoning, yet a principled, model-intrinsic signal that captures its layer-wise reasoning dynamics remains under-explored. We bridge this gap by demonstrating that the L2 norm of hidden states serves as an endogenous signal of the model's reasoning intensity. Using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a diagnostic probe, we observe that LLMs' internal reasoning is marked by a sharp increase in reasoning feature activations concentrated in late layers. Motivated by this pattern, we establish a formal link between reasoning intensity and the model's latent geometry and theoretically prove that the L2 norm of hidden states bounds the activation strength of SAE reasoning features. Empirical correlation analysis and causal interventions further prove L2 norm as a faithful indicator, where heightened norms consistently correspond to critical reasoning steps. We then introduce three test-time scaling techniques guided by L2 norms: (i) Adaptive Layer-wise Reasoning Recursion, (ii) Endogenous Reasoning State Steering, and (iii) L2-guided Response Selection, which requires no additional training or data and is compatible with advanced inference engines. Experiments across model architectures and benchmarks show that L2-norm-based techniques significantly improve reasoning performance, offering a principled yet simple lens to perceive and control LLM latent reasoning dynamics.
bibliography.title: The Tell-Tale Norm: L2 Magnitude as a Signal for Reasoning Dynamics in Large Language Models

contributions: Uses per-layer SAEs and a thinking-versus-non-thinking contrast to identify reasoning features, and shows their activation is concentrated in roughly the final quarter of layers rather than distributed through the network.

Proves under four stated assumptions that the summed differential activation of reasoning features is bounded above and below by the square root of the observed change in squared hidden-state norm, making the norm a two-sided proxy for reasoning feature strength.

Reports Spearman correlations showing the L2 norm tracks SAE reasoning activation and final output entropy far better than layer hidden entropy, layer output entropy or attention entropy, across four models.
Establishes necessity causally: suppressing high-norm hidden states in late layers degrades accuracy far more than suppressing the same proportion of randomly chosen states.
Introduces an adaptive, data-free peak detector based on the interquartile range of the norm sequence within the current decode, which avoids any cross-benchmark threshold.

Builds three training-free test-time methods on that detector -- recursively re-applying a layer at a norm peak, steering a peak state toward a cached earlier high-norm state selected by cosine similarity, and ranking sampled responses by summed late-layer norm -- and evaluates them across seven models and seven benchmarks.
Maps the boundary of the signal: the methods help on reasoning-intensive tasks and consistently hurt on factual-recall ones.
result.limitations: The authors state the central caveat themselves: task difficulty and task domain both shift norm statistics, so the norm is not a one-dimensional characterization of reasoning but reflects a mixture of computational factors whose mechanism is unresolved, and they present the work as evidence that a simple endogenous signal reveals structure rather than as an account of latent reasoning. Their failure-mode analysis is unusually candid and sharpens this: on NQ-Open and PubMedQA the methods consistently degrade performance across both model families, because amplifying deliberation makes a model derive facts it should retrieve, so the same signal that marks productive reasoning marks overthinking on retrieval-style tasks. The practical fragility is the threshold. Every gain depends on the adaptive interquartile detector; a fixed threshold is catastrophic, and there is no universal cutoff because a high norm on GSM8K is a low norm on GPQA. The theory rests on four assumptions -- decoder orthonormality, reconstruction fidelity, semantic-reasoning orthogonality, feature disentanglement -- validated only approximately and empirically, and the reasoning features themselves are defined as whatever differs between thinking and non-thinking responses on one dataset, so what the theorem bounds is that contrast rather than reasoning as such. Improvements are reported as relative percentages throughout, which inflates the apparent size of gains that are two to four absolute points on average, and no seed variance is reported for the main tables. Finally, response selection requires sampling multiple candidates, so its comparison against a single-pass baseline is not compute-matched.
result.method: An independent sparse autoencoder is trained per layer on hidden states collected during inference on MMLU-Pro. Reasoning features are identified by a paired contrast rather than by inspection: the same problem is answered twice, once with an explicit chain of thought and once with a direct answer, and features are ranked by the difference in mean activation between the two token sets, which holds the semantics roughly fixed and isolates what the thinking mode adds. The theory then connects that to geometry. Assuming an approximately orthonormal decoder basis, faithful reconstruction, near-orthogonality between base semantics and a reasoning component, and a partition of features into base and reasoning sets, the squared norm of a hidden state approximates the total energy of its active latent features, and the summed differential activation of reasoning features is sandwiched between constants times the square root of the observed squared-norm gap. Empirically the link is checked three ways: layer-wise trend alignment against SAE activations, Spearman correlation against alternative intrinsic statistics, and a thinking-versus-non-thinking comparison of norms token by token and layer by layer. Necessity is tested by intervention: within the final quarter of layers, any hidden state whose norm exceeds an adaptive per-layer threshold is scaled by 0.1, with random suppression of the same proportion as the control. For control, peaks are detected online as points exceeding the third quartile plus 1.5 times the interquartile range of the norms seen so far in this decode, which is prior-free and adapts to prompt difficulty. Three interventions hang off that detector, and a response-selection rule scores candidates by summed norms over the deepest layers of the last third of generated tokens.
result.one_liner: Argues that the L2 norm of a hidden state is a training-free proxy for how hard a model is reasoning at that layer and token, proves it bounds the activation of SAE-identified reasoning features, and uses norm peaks to decide where to recurse a layer, where to steer, and which sampled response to keep.
result.problem: Signals used to locate reasoning are either retrospective or expensive. Output-level heuristics -- entropy, token rank, mutual information with correctness -- can only mark reasoning after a token is decoded, so they cannot say where in the forward pass computation is happening. Sparse autoencoders can, but they are not endogenous: one has to be trained per layer per model, which is costly and model-specific. What was missing is a quantity already present inside the model that tracks reasoning activity across depth and can therefore be both read and acted on during generation.

relevance.reasoning-interpretability: Proposes an unusually cheap probe and, more valuably for the archive, argues for it in the right order: correlational alignment against alternatives, a theorem bounding what it stands for, and a causal intervention with a matched random control. The comparison table is the durable content -- the L2 norm tracks SAE reasoning features at Spearman 84 to 88 while layer entropy, output entropy and attention entropy all correlate negatively -- because it says which of the cheap internal statistics the archive already holds papers about is worth reading. The honest limit is that reasoning features are operationally defined by a thinking-versus-non-thinking contrast, so the whole construction inherits whatever that contrast conflates; the authors' own conclusion, that the norm is not a one-dimensional characterization, should be carried with the result.
relevance.test-time-scaling: Relocates the compute knob from the output dimension to depth. Rather than generating more tokens, it detects where in the forward pass reasoning is most intense and spends computation there -- re-applying a layer, steering the state, or ranking samples by late-layer norm. Read against the archive's question of how accuracy trades against tokens spent, three findings matter. First, one refinement loop captures nearly all the benefit and eight loops fall below baseline, which is the same diminishing-then-harmful shape seen with extra output tokens, appearing again on a different axis. Second, the gains land on AIME and GPQA and vanish on GSM8K, so the method amplifies reasoning only where reasoning was the bottleneck. Third, and most useful, the failure modes give the boundary explicitly: on retrieval-style tasks the same intervention consistently hurts, so 'more thinking' is a task-conditional good, and a high norm is an overthinking signal exactly when the task wanted recall.

result.results: On Qwen3 at 1.7B through 32B and R1-Distill-Llama at 8B and 70B, over AIME24, AIME25, GSM8K, GSM-Plus, BBH, GPQA-main and MMLU-Pro. The correlation evidence is strong and one-sided: Spearman correlation between layer-wise L2 norm and SAE reasoning activation is 86.47, 85.15, 87.62 and 84.11 on Qwen3-1.7B, 8B, 14B and LLaMA3-8B, against final output entropy 63.52 to 52.10, while the three alternative statistics correlate negatively with SAE activation, from -19.94 to -72.15. Both SAE activation and norm rise sharply in about the last quarter of layers, and thinking generations carry consistently higher norms than non-thinking ones, with the gap widening in later layers. Causally, suppressing high-norm states degrades accuracy severely even at low suppression ratios while random suppression of the same proportion degrades it much less, across all six benchmarks on Qwen3-14B. The three methods give consistent but moderate gains, and the headline figures are relative rather than absolute: the reported +4.51 percent average and +9.13 percent on challenging tasks correspond to average accuracy moving by roughly 2 to 4 points -- for recursion, 57.44 to 61.18 on Qwen3-1.7B, 70.56 to 73.72 on 4B, 78.15 to 80.49 on 32B, 74.56 to 76.47 on LLaMA-70B. Gains concentrate where the analysis predicts: AIME24 rises 60.00 to 70.00 on Qwen3-4B and 40.00 to 48.33 on Qwen3-1.7B, while GSM8K moves by a fraction of a point or slightly down (96.44 to 96.36 on Qwen3-32B). Against other steering signals on Qwen3-4B, the norm-based method leads on AIME, GPQA and MMLU-Pro while an SAE-based steer wins BBH and GSM-Plus; on R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B the SAE steer wins AIME24 and GSM8K, so the claim is robustness across tasks rather than dominance. The sensitivity table is the most informative part: replacing the adaptive threshold with a fixed one collapses AIME24 from 70.00 to 23.33 for recursion and from 66.67 to 16.67 for steering, and running eight refinement loops instead of one drops it to 36.67, below baseline. A single loop already captures most of the benefit, and norms grow past the model's observed maximum after about four loops. The methods are not additive: recursion plus steering is complementary, but steering plus selection is worse than either, because steering distorts the very norm distribution selection ranks on.
